title: Why Goldman Sachs (GS) Stock Is Trading Up Today - StockStory
content: Shares of global investment bank Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) jumped 2.9% in the afternoon session after SpaceX made its market debut (the largest IPO in U.S. history) with Goldman as the lead underwriter. The timing played an important role as CEO David Solomon spent most of his Q1 2026 earnings call predicting what he called a "dealmaking renaissance": an unprecedented surge in IPOs, mergers, and capital markets activity driven by private equity dry powder, deregulation, and stabilizing interest rates. SpaceX, $75 billion raised at a $1.77 trillion valuation, was the most emphatic validation of that thesis to date. The fee economics from a deal of this scale are substantial, and the reputational halo is arguably larger: Goldman cements its position as the bank of first call for generational listings. The Iran peace deal extended the story. Lower oil prices and a delayed Fed rate hike improve exactly the macro environment Solomon said the pipeline needed to open. Two of GS's most anticipated mandates, lead advisory roles on Anthropic and OpenAI, remain ahead. The fundamentals supported the move: Q1 investment banking fees surged 48% year-over-year, revenue reached $17.23 billion against a $16.66 billion estimate, and EPS of $17.55 beat the $15.92 consensus by more than 10%. The shares closed the day at $1,063, up 2.6% from the previous close. Is now the time to buy Goldman Sachs? Access our full analysis report here, it’s free. Goldman Sachs’s shares are not very volatile and have only had 2 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful, although it might not be something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business. The biggest move we wrote about over the last year was 4 months ago when the stock dropped 7.6% on the news that the release of a stronger-than-anticipated Producer Price Index (PPI) report showed wholesale inflation rose more than expected in January. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the PPI, a key measure of inflation at the wholesale level, increased by 0.5% last month, significantly above the 0.3% consensus forecast from economists. On a year-over-year basis, the index rose 2.9%. This unexpectedly high reading suggests that inflationary pressures in the supply chain are more persistent than previously thought. The data has dampened investor optimism for near-term interest rate cuts from the Federal Reserve, as the central bank is less likely to lower borrowing costs while inflation remains elevated. This shift in expectations for monetary policy triggered a broad sell-off across the market, as traders adjusted to the possibility of interest rates remaining higher for longer. Goldman Sachs is up 16.3% since the beginning of the year, and at $1,064 per share, it is trading close to its 52-week high of $1,093 from June 2026. title: BMW F 450 GS Bookings Temporarily Stopped - Motoroids
content: The BMW F 450 GS arrived in India earlier this year and quickly attracted a lot of interest from adventure motorcycle buyers. The motorcycle was launched in April and became one of the most talked-about products in its segment. Now, less than two months after its launch, bookings have reportedly been paused across dealerships. According to dealer sources, the first allocation of the motorcycle has already been fully booked. BMW Motorrad India has not issued an official statement yet, but several dealerships are no longer accepting fresh bookings for the motorcycle. What is interesting is that the booking pause is not limited to one particular version. Among the three, the Trophy version appears to be attracting the most enquiries. That is not surprising because it comes with BMW’s Easy Ride Clutch system and adjustable suspension. Some dealers believe ‘Trophy’ buyers could end up waiting longer than customers opting for the other two variantsCustomers Already Facing Delays People who placed bookings during the initial weeks are also not getting immediate deliveries. Depending on the city, waiting periods are being quoted anywhere between three and four months. In a few places, the timeline is said to be even longer. The exact duration will depend on dealership allocation and future stock arrivals. BMW has equipped the motorcycle with a 420cc parallel-twin liquid-cooled engine that develops 48 bhp. The Trophy variant additionally gets Easy Ride Clutch and adjustable suspension. For now, buyers who were planning to place an order may have to wait until dealerships receive fresh stock. With demand continuing to remain strong, the waiting period is unlikely to disappear anytime soon.

content: WeBearSoft said its SSL/TLS certificate automation management solution, CertBear, has obtained Grade 1 GS (Good Software) certification, the highest level under Korea's national software quality certification system. According to the company, CertBear is an SSL/TLS certificate lifecycle management platform that automatically detects certificates through port scanning by server-based agents and provides integrated management of both public and private certificates. WeBearSoft said the platform automates the entire process from issuance and renewal to deployment, reducing repetitive manual work. The system was designed to enable immediate responses to certificate expiration or errors through real-time monitoring and multi-channel alerts. The company said organizations are seeking to reduce management burdens and minimize risks related to certificate expiration incidents. GS certification is a state-recognized software quality certification system granted by accredited testing institutions including the Korea Testing & Research Institute based on international standards including ISO/IEC 25023, 25041 and 25051. The certification evaluates software across categories including functional suitability, performance efficiency, usability, reliability and security. Grade 1 represents the highest quality level and is considered essential for entry into Korea's public procurement market, including registration on the government procurement platform and preferential purchasing by public institutions.

title: Bunker Rebuilt This R nineT Scrambler to Look Like BMW’s Dakar-Winning R 80 GS - HiConsumption
content:
Our editors carefully select every product we recommend. We may earn a commission from these links. Learn more The custom bike world has a chronic overdesign problem. Too many builds pile on billet parts and wild bodywork until the donor bike disappears entirely. Bunker Custom Cycles, the Istanbul-based outfit run by brothers Mert and Can Uzer, went the opposite direction with this 2024 BMW R nineT Scrambler, and the restraint is exactly what makes it work. The backstory definitely helps, too. The bike belongs to Selçuk, an Istanbul enduro rider who recently became a father and decided hard-charging off-road racing no longer fit the program. He wanted something practical and characterful for lighter adventures. Bunker’s answer was to channel the utilitarian honesty of BMW’s mid-1980s R 80 GS and Dakar machines, bikes whose function dictated their form. The biggest transformation sits right in the middle of the bike. The original steel fuel tank remains underneath, but Bunker designed a custom outer shell that harkens back to the proportions of the old R 80 and R 100 tanks. Capacity does drop slightly, from 4.5 gallons down to 4.1 (15.5 liters), but the visual payoff is huge. The overall aesthetic feels much more cohesive across the board. Up front, the headlight assembly was raised by a little over an inch, then wrapped in a new fairing paired with a high-mounted front fender – both classic Dakar cues. The clever bit is the Denali S4 fog light integrated directly into the fairing. Rather than clamping an auxiliary light to the bars like an afterthought, Bunker baked it into the bodywork. This adds some nice function to the mix while keeping clutter to a minimum. The rest of the bodywork follows suit, and includes a new seat, side panels, intake cover, rear fender, taillight section, and a small luggage rack, all shaped from glass fiber reinforced plastic. Even the skid plate is there to complete the bike’s lower line, not necessarily for bashing rocks. The 1,170cc air/oil-cooled boxer stays bone stock at 109 horsepower, because it didn’t really need fixing. The white paint with red and blue racing accents is a straight nod to BMW’s 1980s motorsport graphics, and the whole thing wears it beautifully. Builder: Bunker Custom Cycles

Engine: 1,170cc air/oil-cooled boxer twin
Power: 109 HP

Auxiliary Lighting: Denali S4 fog light (fairing-integrated)
Livery: White with red and blue racing accents This particular build is a one-off commission, but here’s the good news: Bunker developed most of these parts, including the fairing, high front fender, and rear fender kits, as plug-and-play products. title: Attorney General Ellison secures settlement with GS Labs regarding overpriced and delayed COVID-19 tests - Red Lake Nation News
content:
Babaamaajimowinan (Telling of news in different places) Minnesotans to receive more than $442,000 in restitution June 10, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) - Attorney General Ellison today announced a $4.87 million multistate settlement with GS Labs that resolves claims that the testing company overcharged patients, unlawfully charged administrative fees, and failed to deliver timely COVID-19 test results. A copy of the settlement is attached to this press release. The multistate coalition, co-led by Attorney General Ellison, investigated a number of problems with GS Labs's nationwide testing practices from 2020 through 2022, including that: - GS Labs intentionally advertised inflated "cash prices" for COVID-19 tests, sometimes as high as $380 per test or nearly $1,000 for multi-panel tests, that were used to justify overcharging patients with insurance coverage. And while GS Labs offered a "discount" from these "cash prices" to actual cash-paying patients, almost 30,000 patients still paid much more than market rate for their COVID-19 tests. - For hundreds of thousands of patients, GS Labs guaranteed test results within three days and failed to deliver on its promise, sometimes taking a week or longer to get test results to patients. - Despite advertising that patients with insurance would have no out-of-pocket costs, the company charged administrative fees as high as $49 per test to about 70,000 patients. "I have no patience for pandemic profiteers like GS Labs that deliberately overcharged for COVID-19 tests and deceived Minnesotans about the out-of-pocket costs they would have to pay," said Attorney General Ellison. "It is also disappointing that GS Labs promised test results in three days that actually took a week or more to deliver. I'm sure many Minnesotans made plans to travel, to see family, or to attend events that depended on getting quick COVID-19 test results, and GS Labs' failure to produce quick test results caused significant problems in people's lives. today's settlement holds GS Labs accountable for overcharging consumers and misrepresenting their services." Under the terms of the settlement that was filed today in Ramsey County District Court, GS Labs will pay $3,628,718.34 in restitution to patients, including $1,843,375.99 for cash-paying patients that were overcharged for tests, $1,749,568.35 for patients that were charged administrative fees, and $33,692 for cash-paying patients that did not receive test results within three days. Minnesotans that were harmed by GS Labs's testing practices will receive $442,847.50 in restitution through the settlement. The settlement creates an online restitution mechanism that will be funded and administered by GS Labs, with oversight by the multistate coalition. Eligible consumers include out-of-pocket paying consumers who paid in excess of the market rate for testing, consumers who paid for test results that were not delivered within the advertised turn-around time, and consumers who paid administrative fees to GS Labs. To determine one's eligibility and, if applicable, to receive a restitution payment, consumers must complete a brief verification process, which is available at http://www.gslabstesting.com. All information used to verify a consumer's identity will solely be used for that purpose and will not be saved, stored or shared. The refund process involves digital security that will ensure the safety of any submitted information. Consumers are encouraged to complete this process as soon as possible, as restitution payments will be processed on a rolling basis. GS Labs will be contacting affected consumers via email to share more information about the restitution process. The company will also pay $1.25 million to the multistate group, which includes a payment of $146,531.65 to Minnesota. GS Labs has represented to the States that it no longer offers testing services and is not operational. As part of the settlement, if GS Labs decides to resume testing services, the company must make several changes to its advertising and sales practices, including: - GS Labs must disclose in its marketing materials the maximum time for it to disclose test results. - GS Labs will report testing results within the advertised time period and, if it cannot, it must notify patients of the delay and offer a full refund. - GS Labs must comply with local, state, and federal requirements to promptly deliver COVID-19 test results and provide notification of any delays. - GS Labs will cease charging cash-paying patients fees in excess of market rates, charging patients for late test results, and charging administrative fees in violation of state and federal laws. - GS Labs must disclose in its marketing materials the actual cash price that will be charged to patients, including clearly disclosing any applicable discounts. - GS Labs cannot charge administrative fees for COVID-19 testing services. - GS Labs cannot unjustifiably increase the cost of its testing services during a declared emergency. Along with Minnesota, the settlement was negotiated by Kansas, Nebraska, and Washington. Joining the settlement are the Attorneys General of Alabama, Arizona, Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, and South Dakota. title: GS Labs ordered to pay $4.87 million to 18 states - including Nebraska, Iowa - in COVID test settlement - WOWT
content:
LINCOLN, Neb. (WOWT) - Nebraska and Iowa are among 18 states that will get a share of nearly $5 million in a settlement with GS Labs over allegations of overpriced and delayed COVID-19 tests at the height of the pandemic. The lawsuit filed by 18 states said GS Labs overcharged patients whose tests were covered by health insurance. Claims filed against the testing company alleged they had charged patients as much as $380 per test to nearly $1,000 for “multi-panel” tests despite advertising no out-of-pocket costs. In 2021, three clients sent First Alert 6 their medical insurance statements showing COVID-19 testing lab bills of $1,500, $1,600, and $2,000. In a response to First Alert 6 on Wednesday, GS Labs “expressly denies the allegations”: “GS Labs was founded in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and ultimately tested more than 1.4 million Americans, identifying approximately 200,000 positive cases. At its peak, GS Labs handled 20–30% of the rapid testing market in states such as Minnesota and Washington. The settlement expressly denies the allegations against GS Labs, and we agreed to resolve the matter to bring a years-long investigation to a close — not because we believe the claims have merit. We remain proud of our more than 3,000 employees, including many led by U.S. military veterans and many who had been displaced by pandemic shutdowns. They kept testing sites open, supported local jobs and communities, and showed up every day during one of the most chaotic periods in modern public health." The $4.87 million settlement includes $3.6 million in restitution to patients: $1.8 million for cash-paying patients who were overcharged for tests, $1.75 million for patients charged administrative fees, and $33,692 for cash-paying patients who didn’t get their test results within three days. In December 2020, a First Alert 6 investigation found that hundreds of COVID GS Labs test results had been delayed. At the time, GS Labs blamed subcontractors ImmunoGenomics and Quest Labs for the hold up. The rest of the settlement, about $1.25 million, will be dispersed to the states in varying amounts. In a news Wednesday news release, Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said the state will receive $368,403 from that portion of the settlement, bringing the total headed to Nebraska to nearly $1.5 million. “Companies that take advantage of consumers during a difficult time during a pandemic need to be held accountable. GS Labs significantly overcharged Nebraskans for COVID tests. I’m proud of the work of our office alongside our partnering states to negotiate this settlement for consumers,” Hilgers said in a statement. Iowa AG Brenna Bird confirmed that state will get $654,335. From that total, $430,314 will go to Iowans who were charged administrative fees; $59,589 will go to cash-paying Iowans who were overcharged for tests; and $1,751 will be available for Iowans who didn’t receive their test results within three days. The rest — about $163,000 — is Iowa’s share of the $1.25 million payout to the states. “Not only did GS Labs profit by taking advantage of Iowans, but they did so during a national health crisis when many were facing serious health challenges,” Bird said in the Iowa release. “I’m grateful for the work that secured restitution for affected Iowans, and I will continue to protect Iowa consumers from unfair and deceptive practices.” Hilgers and AGs from Kansas, Minnesota, and Washington negotiated the settlement. Other states attaching to the filing, in addition to Iowa, include Alabama, Arizona, Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, and South Dakota. Those who believe they are eligible for a refund can submit requests online through the GS Labs website. The company’s compliance will be monitored by the state coalition participating in the lawsuit. Payments will be processed on a rolling basis, so those who believe they qualify are encouraged to complete their refund requests as soon as possible. GS Labs will then contact them via email with more information about the restitution process. While GS Labs is no longer operational, the company has agreed to adhere to certain advertising and sales policies if it ever resumes testing services. title: Iowa AG: GS Labs to pay $4.87M in multistate COVID-19 testing overcharge settlement - KGAN
content: DES Moines, Iowa — Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird announced Wednesday that GS Labs has agreed to a $4.87 million multistate settlement over allegations that the COVID-19 testing company overcharged patients, imposed unlawful fees and failed to deliver test results within promised timeframes during the pandemic. The settlement resolves claims that GS Labs engaged in deceptive business practices between 2020 and 2022 while providing COVID-19 testing services across multiple states. According to the attorneys general involved in the investigation, GS Labs advertised inflated cash prices that were used to justify higher charges to insured patients, charged nearly 30,000 consumers above market rates for COVID-19 tests and failed to provide results within its advertised three-day window. Investigators alleged some patients waited a week or longer to receive results. The states also alleged that despite advertising no out-of-pocket costs for insured patients, GS Labs charged administrative fees of up to $49 per test to approximately 70,000 consumers. “Not only did GS Labs profit by taking advantage of Iowans, but they did so during a national health crisis when many were facing serious health challenges,” Bird said in a statement. “I’m grateful for the work that secured restitution for affected Iowans, and I will continue to protect Iowa consumers from unfair and deceptive practices.” Under the settlement, GS Labs will pay more than $3.6 million in restitution to affected consumers across the participating states. Iowa consumers are eligible for approximately $491,655 in reimbursement, including about $430,314 for administrative fees, nearly $59,589 for alleged overcharges to cash-paying patients and about $1,752 for delayed test results. Eligible Iowa consumers can seek reimbursement through an online claims process at gslabstesting.com. The attorney general’s office said payments will be issued on a rolling basis, and GS Labs will contact affected consumers by email with additional information about the reimbursement process. In addition to consumer restitution, GS Labs will pay $1.25 million to the coalition of states involved in the settlement, including about $162,681 to Iowa. GS Labs has told the states that it is no longer operating and does not currently provide testing services. Under the agreement, if the company resumes testing operations in the future, it must implement changes to its advertising and sales practices to comply with state consumer protection laws. The settlement includes Iowa and the attorneys general of Alabama, Arizona, Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Dakota and Washington.

title: Iowans gets share of $5 million settlement for overpriced COVID tests - The Des Moines Register
content: A medical testing company is paying nearly $5 million to settle claims that it overcharged for tests during the COVID-19 pandemic, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird says. Omaha-based GS Labs was founded in October 2020 to provide COVID tests, according to the now-defunct company's website. In a Wednesday, June 10, news release, Bird accused the company of charging almost 30,000 patients above-market prices for the tests and billing 70,000 insured patients administrative fees of up to $49 despite advertising no out-of-pocket costs. The company also failed to provide results within three days as promised, the release said. Iowa is among 20 states that sued GS Labs. Under the settlement, the company will pay the states $1.25 million, with Iowa's share exceeding $160,000, and reimburse consumers more than $3.62 million, nearly $500,000 of which will go to Iowans. "Not only did GS Labs profit by taking advantage of Iowans, but they did so during a national health crisis when many were facing serious health challenges,” Bird said in a statement. “I’m grateful for the work that secured restitution for affected Iowans, and I will continue to protect Iowa consumers from unfair and deceptive practices.” Iowans seeking reimbursements can begin the online settlement process at gslabstesting.com, according to Bird's office. GS Labs also will email affected consumers. William Morris covers courts for the Des Moines Register. He can be contacted at wrmorris2@registermedia.com or 715-573-8166.

title: Settlement to provide nearly $1M in restitution to Washington COVID-19 testers - KOMO
content: How much restitution will Washington residents receive from GS Labs? How does this settlement reflect consumer protection trends? What Medicaid work requirements could impact coverage? SEATTLE — Washington residents who paid for COVID-19 tests through GS Labs during the pandemic could soon receive a share of nearly $1 million in restitution under a bipartisan multistate settlement that resolves claims the company overcharged patients and failed to deliver timely results. The settlement stems from an 18-state investigation into GS Labs’ nationwide testing practices from 2020 through 2022. SEE ALSO | New COVID 'cicada' variant spreads to 25 states: What to know The coalition, co-led by Washington, found multiple issues, including allegations that GS Labs advertised inflated “cash prices” for COVID-19 tests — sometimes as high as $380 per test or nearly $1,000 for multi-panel tests — and used those prices to justify higher charges to insured patients. While the company offered a “discount” from those “cash prices” to people paying out of pocket, the states said almost 30,000 patients still paid much more than the market rate. The coalition also found that for hundreds of thousands of patients, GS Labs guaranteed test results within three days but did not meet that promise, sometimes taking a week or longer. In addition, despite advertising that patients with insurance would have no out-of-pocket costs, the company charged administrative fees as high as $49 per test to about 70,000 patients, according to the settlement information. “During the height of the pandemic, GS Labs unfairly profited off of Washingtonians just trying to get tested for COVID-19,” Attorney General Nick Brown said. “This is another great example of how our office vigorously enforces Washington’s consumer protection laws to protect people from deceptive business practices.” Under the terms of the settlement, GS Labs will pay a total of $3.6 million in restitution to patients in the 18 plaintiff states. That includes $1.8 million for cash-paying patients who were overcharged for tests, $1.75 million for patients who were charged administrative fees, and about $34,000 for cash-paying patients who did not receive test results within three days. In Washington, more than $987,000 will be available to compensate residents harmed by the company’s testing practices. More than 11,000 people in the state are expected to qualify for restitution, with payments ranging from $5 for people who were improperly charged administrative fees to $200 for people who paid for a COVID test out of pocket. SEE ALSO | Seattle businesses under more financial strain now than at the COVID pandemic's peak The settlement creates an online restitution process funded and administered by GS Labs, with oversight by the multistate coalition. Eligible consumers include out-of-pocket paying consumers who paid more than the market rate for testing, consumers who paid for test results that were not delivered within the advertised turnaround time, and consumers who paid administrative fees to GS Labs. To check eligibility and receive a payment, consumers must complete a brief verification process at www.gslabstesting.com. Restitution payments will be processed on a rolling basis, and consumers are encouraged to complete the process as soon as possible. GS Labs will contact affected consumers by email with more information about the restitution process. GS Labs has represented to the states that it no longer offers testing services and is not operational. The settlement also sets requirements if the company resumes testing, including disclosing the maximum time to provide results, reporting results within the advertised time period, notifying patients of delays and offering a full refund, and complying with local, state, and federal requirements for prompt delivery and delay notifications. If it returns to testing, GS Labs also must stop charging cash-paying patients more than market rates, stop charging for late test results, stop charging administrative fees in violation of state and federal laws, clearly disclose the actual cash price and any discounts in marketing materials, and it cannot charge administrative fees for COVID-19 testing services. The settlement also bars unjustified price increases during a declared emergency.

title: Overcharged for a COVID test in Minnesota? You may get money back - KIMT
content: SAINT PAUL, Minn. — Attorney General Keith Ellison announced a $4.87 million multistate settlement with GS Labs that resolves claims the testing company overcharged patients, unlawfully charged administrative fees and failed to deliver timely COVID-19 test results. The multistate coalition, co-led by Ellison, investigated problems with GS Labs' nationwide testing practices from 2020 through 2022. Ellison says the company intentionally advertised inflated cash prices for COVID-19 tests, sometimes as high as $380 per test or nearly $1,000 for multi-panel tests, that were used to justify overcharging patients with insurance coverage. Almost 30,000 patients paid much more than market rate for their COVID-19 tests. For hundreds of thousands of patients, GS Labs allegedly guaranteed test results within three days and failed to deliver on its promise, sometimes taking a week or longer to get test results to patients. Despite advertising that patients with insurance would have no out-of-pocket costs, the company charged administrative fees as high as $49 per test to about 70,000 patients. "I have no patience for pandemic profiteers like GS Labs that deliberately overcharged for COVID-19 tests and deceived Minnesotans about the out-of-pocket costs they would have to pay," Ellison said. "It is also disappointing that GS Labs promised test results in three days that actually took a week or more to deliver." "I'm sure many Minnesotans made plans to travel, to see family, or to attend events that depended on getting quick COVID-19 test results, and GS Labs' failure to produce quick test results caused significant problems in people's lives," Ellison said. "Today's settlement holds GS Labs accountable for overcharging consumers and misrepresenting their services." Under the terms of the settlement filed in Ramsey County District Court, GS Labs will pay more than $3.6 million in restitution to patients. This includes more than $1.8 million for cash-paying patients that were overcharged for tests, more than $1.7 million for patients that were charged administrative fees and $33,692 for cash-paying patients that did not receive test results within three days. Minnesotans that were harmed by GS Labs' testing practices will receive $442,847.50 in restitution through the settlement. The settlement creates an online restitution mechanism that will be funded and run by GS Labs, with oversight by the multistate coalition. Eligible consumers include out-of-pocket paying consumers who paid in excess of the market rate for testing, consumers who paid for test results that were not delivered within the advertised turn-around time and consumers who paid administrative fees to GS Labs. To determine eligibility and receive a restitution payment, consumers must complete a brief verification process at www.gslabstesting.com. The company will also pay $1.25 million to the multistate group, which includes a payment of $146,531.65 to Minnesota. GS Labs has told the states that it no longer offers testing services and is not operational. As part of the settlement, if GS Labs decides to resume testing services, the company must make several changes to its advertising and sales practices. GS Labs must disclose in its marketing materials the maximum time for it to disclose test results. The company will report testing results within the advertised time period and, if it cannot, it must notify patients of the delay and offer a full refund. GS Labs must comply with local, state and federal requirements to promptly deliver COVID-19 test results and provide notification of any delays. GS Labs will stop charging cash-paying patients fees in excess of market rates, charging patients for late test results and charging administrative fees in violation of state and federal laws. The company must disclose in its marketing materials the actual cash price that will be charged to patients, including clearly disclosing any applicable discounts. GS Labs cannot charge administrative fees for COVID-19 testing services or unjustifiably increase the cost of its testing services during a declared emergency. Along with Minnesota, the settlement was negotiated by Kansas, Nebraska and Washington. Joining the settlement are the attorneys general of Alabama, Arizona, Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania and South Dakota. title: OPM Proposes Ending Time-in-Grade Rules for GS Promotions - Clearance Jobs
content: The Office of Personnel Management has released a significant new proposal that would eliminate the long‑standing Time‑in‑Grade (TIG) requirement for General Schedule promotions. If finalized, this change would remove the mandatory 52‑week service requirement at each grade level for GS‑5 and above—one of the most notable updates to federal promotion policy in decades. OPM describes the TIG rule as an outdated safeguard from an earlier era of federal personnel management. While originally designed to prevent favoritism and ensure fairness, the agency now argues that today’s structured merit‑based systems already provide the necessary protections. According to OPM, removing TIG would allow agencies to promote employees based on demonstrated readiness rather than time served, helping modernize the federal career ladder. The proposal is currently open for public comment through July 27, and supports the President’s Executive Order to reform the federal hiring process. Under the proposed rule, TIG would no longer be a factor in determining promotion eligibility. Employees would still need to meet all qualification standards and demonstrate the ability to perform at the higher grade, but agencies would gain the flexibility to promote individuals as soon as they are prepared for increased responsibility. If adopted, the rule could reshape the promotion experience across government. Many employees may see earlier opportunities for advancement, especially in career fields where skills develop rapidly. However, the impact may vary by agency. Some organizations may embrace faster promotions, while others may continue to apply conservative internal policies. Importantly, the proposal does not change qualification standards, competitive merit procedures, or the requirement to demonstrate the ability to perform at the higher grade. Agencies must still follow all merit system principles and ensure fair, transparent promotion processes. The proposal is now in the public comment phase. Federal employees, unions, and agencies are encouraged to review the details and submit feedback through the Federal Register.
